questions.problem:
Find the missing values in the following truth table:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A⇔B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | {{field-1}} |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | {{field-2}} |
questions.worked_solution:
According to the definition of the biconditional, 

- $A⇔B$ is true if $A⇒B$ **and** $B⇒A.$ Otherwise, it is false.

- In other words, $A⇔B$ is true if $A$ and $B$ have the same truth values. Otherwise, it is false.

The complete truth table is shown below:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A⇔B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |

questions.problem: If $A$ is false and $B$ is false, then $A⇔B$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
According to the definition of the biconditional, 

- $A⇔B$ is true if $A⇒B$ **and** $B⇒A.$ Otherwise, it is false.

- In other words, $A⇔B$ is true if $A$ and $B$ have the same truth values. Otherwise, it is false.

So, when $A=\text{F}$ and $B=\text{F},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(A⇔B) & =(\text{F}⇔\text{F}) \\  & =\text{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

The complete truth table is shown below:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A⇔B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{T}$ |
| $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ | $\text{F}$ |
|  |  |  |
| $\text{F}$ | $\text{F}$ | $\text{T}$ |

canonical_examples.problem: If $A$ is true and $B$ is true, what is the truth value of $A \Leftrightarrow B ?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
According to the definition of the biconditional, 

- $A \Leftrightarrow B$ is true if $A\Rightarrow B$ **and** $B\Rightarrow A.$ Otherwise, it is false.

- In other words, $A \Leftrightarrow B$ is true if $A$ and $B$ have the same truth values. Otherwise, it is false.

So, when $A = \textrm T$ and $B = \textrm T,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(A⇔B) & =(\text{T}⇔\text{T}) \\  & =\text{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

The complete truth table is shown below:

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\,A \Leftrightarrow B\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  |  |  |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |

canonical_examples.problem:
Express the following statement as a conjunction of implications.

$$
\neg P \Leftrightarrow Q
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
According to the definition of the biconditional, 

- $A \Leftrightarrow B$ is true if $A\Rightarrow B$ **and** $B\Rightarrow A.$ Otherwise, it is false.

- In other words, $A \Leftrightarrow B$ is true if $A$ and $B$ have the same truth values. Otherwise, it is false.

Therefore, in this case, we have

$$
\neg P \Leftrightarrow Q \equiv (\neg P \Rightarrow Q) \land (Q \Rightarrow \neg P).
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following statements are equivalent to $\lnot (\neg Y \Leftrightarrow Z)?$

- $Y \Rightarrow \lnot Z$

- $(Y \lor Z) \Rightarrow (Y \land Z)$

- $(Y \land Z) \land (Y \land \lnot Z)$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we use the definition of the biconditional statement to write the equivalence as a conjunction of implications: 

$$
\lnot (\lnot Y \Leftrightarrow Z) 
\equiv \lnot \big[(\lnot Y \Rightarrow Z) \land (Z \Rightarrow \lnot Y)\big]
$$

Now, we represent all the implications using disjunctions and negations:

$$
\lnot \big[(\lnot Y \Rightarrow Z) \land (Z \Rightarrow \lnot Y)\big]
\equiv \lnot \big[(\lnot \lnot Y \lor Z) \land (\lnot Z \lor \lnot Y)\big]
$$

Next, we simplify the double negations:

$$
\lnot \big[(\lnot \lnot Y \lor Z) \land (\lnot Z \lor \lnot Y)\big] 
\equiv \lnot \big[(Y \lor Z) \land (\lnot Z \lor \lnot Y)\big]
$$

Now, we use De Morgan's laws:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬[(Y∨Z)∧(¬Z∨¬Y)] & ≡¬(Y∨Z)∨¬(¬Z∨¬Y) \\  & ≡¬(Y∨Z)∨¬¬(Z∧Y)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we again simplify the double negations and write down symbols in alphabetic order inside the parentheses using commutative laws:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(Y∨Z)∨¬¬(Z∧Y) & ≡¬(Y∨Z)∨(Z∧Y) \\  & ≡¬(Y∨Z)∨(Y∧Z) \\  & ≡(Y∨Z)⇒(Y∧Z)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is only II.
